scope: Curated educational guidance from public NASA Human Research Program pages. These are research summaries, not patient datasets, diagnoses, or mission medical procedures. AstroLife is not a validated medical device.
priority_note: NASA describes mission-dependent risks, not a universal ranked list. AstroLife brings reported symptoms and concerns to the top; prevention topics remain visible even when fingertip readings look normal. A priority is an app follow-up prompt, not an estimated probability of disease.

sources.title: NASA: Five hazards of human spaceflight
NASA: Behavioral changes and psychiatric disorders
NASA: Injury and performance during spacewalks
NASA: Hazard: hostile and closed environments
MedlinePlus: Pulse Oximetry (general reference, not a spaceflight threshold)

conditions.title: Low oxygen / hypoxia concern
conditions.why_it_matters: Reduced-pressure habitats can lower oxygen availability and affect thinking, vision, and sleep.
conditions.priority_rationale: Oxygen readings and reported breathing concerns deserve timely review. NASA describes planned mild hypoxia exposure as relatively low risk; an abnormal reading is not a diagnosis.
conditions.monitoring: Record SpO2, measurement quality, symptoms, and activity context; have trained crew review habitat and suit oxygen/pressure data when relevant.
conditions.limitations: A fingertip estimate cannot diagnose hypoxia, establish a safe spacecraft atmosphere, or exclude a problem when symptoms are present.

countermeasures.text: Have trained crew follow the mission's oxygen and pressure procedures and arrange medical review of symptoms or unexpected readings.

research.text: NASA is studying reduced-pressure exposure and suit-pressure options; these are not instructions to adjust oxygen or pressure yourself.

conditions.title: Cardiovascular changes
conditions.why_it_matters: Spaceflight can change circulation and increase concerns about fainting, abnormal rhythms, and blood clots, especially on longer missions.
conditions.priority_rationale: Heart-rate observations can prompt follow-up, while fainting or chest symptoms require clinical assessment regardless of the sensor result.
conditions.monitoring: Log resting heart rate, activity context, dizziness, and fainting; clinicians may need blood pressure, ECG, or ultrasound.
conditions.limitations: Pulse readings cannot diagnose an arrhythmia, blood clot, blood-pressure disorder, or cardiovascular disease.

countermeasures.text: Keep to the crew's prescribed exercise and nutrition plan to support cardiovascular fitness.
Use pre-landing fluid and compression plans only as directed by the mission medical team.

research.text: Research is examining blood-flow and clotting changes and preparation for cardiovascular emergencies on deep-space missions.

conditions.title: Muscle loss and reduced fitness
conditions.why_it_matters: Weightlessness can reduce strength and aerobic capacity, making mission tasks harder and increasing injury risk.
conditions.priority_rationale: Prevention matters throughout a mission even without symptoms; task readiness cannot be inferred from normal pulse or oxygen readings.
conditions.monitoring: Record missed exercise sessions, weakness, fatigue, and difficulty completing usual tasks; use crew fitness evaluations for actual performance measures.
conditions.limitations: AstroLife does not measure muscle mass, strength, aerobic capacity, or readiness for a spacewalk.

countermeasures.text: Follow the individually prescribed resistance and aerobic exercise schedule and periodic fitness assessments.

research.text: Zero T2 tests exercise without a treadmill; CIPHER studies changes across body systems. Neither establishes an exercise prescription for this user.

conditions.title: Bone loss and fracture risk
conditions.why_it_matters: Reduced loading in microgravity weakens bones and can increase fracture risk; changes may be silent.
conditions.priority_rationale: Bone health needs preventive follow-up on long missions and during return to gravity, even when fingertip measurements are reassuring.
conditions.monitoring: Record exercise adherence, pain, and injuries. Clinical bone scans before and after flight assess bone density.
conditions.limitations: Fingertip sensors and symptom check-ins cannot measure bone density or rule out a fracture.

countermeasures.text: Follow the mission's resistance exercise plan and scheduled bone-health reviews.

research.text: NASA studies longer-term bone changes and medical countermeasures. Bone-loss medication requires an individualized clinical decision.

conditions.title: Vision changes / SANS
conditions.why_it_matters: Headward fluid shifts in weightlessness can change the eyes and brain; long-term consequences remain under investigation.
conditions.priority_rationale: NASA identifies SANS as a major research priority for long missions. New visual changes warrant review without relying on fingertip measurements.
conditions.monitoring: Record blurred or changed vision and headaches; arrange mission eye examinations and imaging when indicated.
conditions.limitations: A photo, pulse reading, or normal SpO2 cannot diagnose or exclude SANS. Symptoms alone do not establish SANS.

countermeasures.text: Report new visual changes to the medical team and follow the planned eye-monitoring schedule.

research.text: B-Complex and Thigh Cuff investigate possible countermeasures for space-related eye changes. Supplements and cuffs are investigational, not self-treatment recommendations.

conditions.title: Dizziness and motion sickness
conditions.why_it_matters: Gravity transitions can disrupt orientation, coordination, and motion tolerance, affecting safe movement and vehicle operation.
conditions.priority_rationale: Balance and orientation concerns matter most around gravity transitions and tasks that demand coordination.
conditions.monitoring: Record dizziness, nausea, balance problems, and timing relative to landing or other gravity transitions.
conditions.limitations: Fingertip measurements cannot identify the cause of dizziness or assess vestibular function.

countermeasures.text: Tell the crew about disorientation and use the mission's trained assistance and task-readiness procedures before demanding movement or piloting.

research.text: NASA is evaluating orientation training, recovery aids, and motion-sickness medicines. Medication choices belong with the medical team.

conditions.title: Sleep loss and fatigue
conditions.why_it_matters: Disrupted light cycles, sleep loss, and heavy workloads can impair health and mission performance.
conditions.priority_rationale: Daily sleep and fatigue reports help identify concerns before they interfere with demanding tasks.
conditions.monitoring: Track sleep duration, perceived sleep quality, fatigue, and work/rest disruption.
conditions.limitations: Check-ins are self-reports; a fingertip reading does not establish sleep quality or fitness for duty.

countermeasures.text: Protect scheduled sleep and recovery time and follow the mission's day/night lighting plan.
Discuss persistent fatigue and workload adjustments with the crew lead or medical team.

research.text: ARCHeR monitored sleep, activity, and well-being on Artemis II; it is a research study, not a validated AstroLife fatigue model.

conditions.title: Behavioral health and teamwork
conditions.why_it_matters: Isolation and confinement can affect mood and decisions; communication delays make support and team coordination harder.
conditions.priority_rationale: Stress, mood concerns, and conflict can affect safety even when physiological readings are unremarkable.
conditions.monitoring: Record perceived stress, mood concerns, isolation, and team friction; seek a private conversation with the appropriate support professional.
conditions.limitations: Self-reports and pulse readings cannot diagnose a psychiatric disorder or measure team effectiveness.

countermeasures.text: Maintain planned contact with family and behavioral-health support; use protected self-care time or journaling.
Use practiced team communication and conflict-resolution routines; raise unresolved strain with the crew lead.

research.text: Ground-based isolation studies test support strategies, privacy needs, and how teams adapt during long missions.

conditions.title: Immune changes and infection concerns
conditions.why_it_matters: Spaceflight stressors can alter immunity and reactivate dormant viruses; changes in microbes may also affect illness risk.
conditions.priority_rationale: New illness or skin symptoms need review in a shared habitat; normal vitals do not exclude infection or immune changes.
conditions.monitoring: Log feverishness, rashes, sores, and new illness symptoms; clinical samples and environmental sampling provide different information.
conditions.limitations: The app cannot measure immune function, identify a pathogen, or diagnose infection from a photo.

countermeasures.text: Follow crew infection-prevention and environmental-sampling procedures, and report new illness to the medical team.
Follow preflight exposure-limiting precautions set by the mission team.

research.text: Immune Biomarkers examined Artemis II blood and saliva samples. Such laboratory research does not validate immunity estimates from fingertip readings.

conditions.title: Inadequate nutrition
conditions.why_it_matters: Food must remain safe, nutritious, and appealing through long missions with limited resupply.
conditions.priority_rationale: Poor intake or appetite deserves follow-up because it can undermine health and performance across multiple body systems.
conditions.monitoring: Record missed meals, poor appetite, and difficulty following the assigned food plan; review intake with the nutrition team.
conditions.limitations: Pulse and SpO2 do not measure hydration, energy balance, vitamin status, or malnutrition.

countermeasures.text: Follow the mission nutrition plan and report foods that are unavailable, poorly tolerated, or unappealing so the team can adjust the menu.

research.text: NASA is improving diet quality, food variety, and shelf life for longer missions; these studies do not justify unsupervised supplementation.

conditions.title: Spacewalk injury and decompression concerns
conditions.why_it_matters: Pressure transitions can cause decompression sickness; suit work also creates physical and cognitive strain.
conditions.priority_rationale: Symptoms during or after an EVA or pressure change need prompt mission-team review, even with normal fingertip readings.
conditions.monitoring: Record recent spacewalks or pressure changes, pain, unusual fatigue, and breathing or neurological symptoms; use suit telemetry and crew medical assessment.
conditions.limitations: SpO2 does not detect nitrogen bubbles, exclude decompression sickness, measure carbon dioxide, or clear a crew member for an EVA.

countermeasures.text: Use the approved prebreathe, suit-check, and EVA fitness procedures under trained crew supervision.
For suspected decompression symptoms, alert the crew and follow the mission procedure to safely end the EVA and return to a pressurized environment.

research.text: Variable-pressure suits and habitat-atmosphere designs are under study. Pressure changes require mission authority, not app instructions.

conditions.title: Radiation exposure and long-term health
conditions.why_it_matters: Space radiation can increase cancer risk and may harm the nervous, cardiovascular, and other systems, particularly beyond Earth's shielding.
conditions.priority_rationale: This major exploration hazard must stay visible despite being undetectable by the fingertip sensor and often not immediately perceptible.
conditions.monitoring: Use approved personal or vehicle dosimetry, radiation alerts, exposure records, and scheduled medical surveillance.
conditions.limitations: Heart rate, SpO2, symptoms, and photos cannot quantify radiation dose or rule out radiation-related harm.

countermeasures.text: Follow mission radiation alerts, shielding or shelter procedures, exposure monitoring, and medical follow-up plans.

research.text: NASA studies better shielding, personalized risk estimates, and possible drug countermeasures. No protective medication is prescribed by this app.

conditions.title: Medical readiness and landing injury
conditions.why_it_matters: Delayed Earth support increases the need for onboard capability. Landing forces and weakened bones or muscles also create injury risk.
conditions.priority_rationale: Medical readiness supports every condition; landing and injury concerns need clinical review rather than clearance from a simple sensor.
conditions.monitoring: Record injuries and new functional difficulties; maintain accessible medical procedures, equipment status, and a health log for the crew medical officer.
conditions.limitations: AstroLife cannot examine injuries, verify medical supplies, replace trained care, or certify vehicle and restraint safety.

countermeasures.text: Keep approved offline procedures available and practice the mission's medical and equipment-response training before it is needed.
Use approved seating, restraints, and landing or egress assistance procedures; report pain or injury to the medical team.

research.text: NASA uses body models to improve landing protection and develops systems crews can operate with less immediate ground support.
